statement:
# BST Height

    The height of a tree is the size of the longest path between the root and all the leaves.

    Write a program that reads the numbers to be added to a BST and
    prints the height of the tree resulting from these insertions.


    ## Input

    Your program should read only one line containing (in order) the elements to be added to the tree.

    You can assume that there will be no repeated elements in the tree.
    You can assume that at least one value is read.

    ## Output

    Your program should print the value of the tree's height.

## Execution examples
    
        $ javac Solution.java; java Solution

        10 8 1 9 20 18 25
        2

question: tree_height
statement:
# Height of a Tree
    
    Although trees such as BSTs and AVLs have a root, a node is considered the “point of origin” of the tree,
    not every tree is rooted. For this problem, let's consider a tree that has no root
    (unrooted).
    
    The height of a tree is the greatest distance from a given node to any other node. Where the distance is
    defined by the number of edges that must be traversed to get from one node to another.
    
    To make it clearer, look at the example below.

    ![Tree](http://www.dsc.ufcg.edu.br/~jarthur/figuras_tst_eda/mari_tree_height.png)
    
The height of the tree above is 3, which is the distance between nodes 2 and 5.
    
    Write a program that reads the definition of an undirected tree and prints the height of the tree and the

    nodes that define this height (i.e. the two furthest nodes and the distance between them).
    
    **Tip: ** think first about how to find the farthest node from a given node, and then how to generalize to find
    the two most distant nodes (height).
    
    **Obs: ** It is guaranteed that there is only one solution, i.e. there are only two nodes whose distance is maximum.

    ## Input

    The first line will contain a single integer N, the number of nodes in the tree.
    Each node is identified with a value from 0 to N-1. The next N-1 lines (think a bit about why N-1?) will
    contain 2 integers representing the edges of the tree. Each edge is represented by two nodes A and B (0 <= A, B <= N-1).

    ## Output

    Your program should print a line in the output containing “from -> X to -> Y height -> H”, without quotes where
    H is the height of the tree, X and Y (X <= Y) are nodes such that the distance between X and Y is equal to the height.
    
    ## Example of execution
    
        $ javac Solution.java; java Solution
        5
        0 1
        0 2
        0 3
        2 4
        from -> 1 to -> 4 height -> 3

    ## Restrictions

question: element_at_stack
statement:
# Element at Stack
    
    Write a program that returns the element at a given index of a stack.
    
    ## Input

    Your program should read two lines of standard input. One line representing the elements
    to be added to the stack in sequence and one line representing the index to be inspected.
    
    You can only use push, pop and other auxiliary structure. The stack must
    retain its initial configuration after the execution of your algorithm. You cannot use `array[index]`
    to access an arbitrary position in the array.
  
    Important: you must consider that the element at the top is at index 0, below it is the element
    at index 1 and so on. 

    ## Output

    Your program should print the element present at the index read. If the index is invalid, print `index invalid`.
    

    ## Examples
    
        javac Solution.java; java Solution
        8 2 3 4 1 5 33 21
        0
        8
       
        javac Solution.java; java Solution
        8 2 3 4 1 5 33 21
        2
        3

        javac Solution.java; java Solution
        8 2 3
        5
        invalid index

    ## Restrictions
    
    You can only use the standard methods of the stack interface (e.g. `peek`, `push`, `pop`, `isEmpty` etc) and other auxiliary structure. 
    The stack must retain its initial configuration after your algorithm is executed.
    
    
    If your stack is based on arrays, you can't access an arbitrary index using stack[index], for example. All access must be done via pop, push and peek.

    Write a **recursive** program that finds the element that breaks an ordered sequence.

        1 2 4 5 3 7 90

    ordered up to it and the value 3 “breaks” this ordering.

    *Important!* There is only one element that breaks the sequence. As said before, 
    as soon as you find it, return the index of that element.

    ## Input

    Your program should read a sequence of space-separated integers.

    ## Output

        -1

    Your program should only manipulate the array of integers.

        - remove
        - pop

statement:
# HashSet

    HashSets implement the mathematical notion of a set in Java, i.e. they don't allow repeated elements. 
    HashSets are very similar to HashTables in terms of implementation, as they can also be based on arrays and 
    use hash functions to determine where to store the value passed in. 
    However, one major difference is that they do **not** store key-value pairs, but only the 
    only the values. 

    Due to the nature of the hash functions we use when building HashSets, collisions are
    inevitable. That is, for some pair of values, there is a possibility that their
    their hashes are the same and, consequently, these objects will be mapped to the same
    position.

    One of the ways to resolve collisions is, if the hash is mapped to an already occupied position the insertion algorithm looks for another free position to insert the value. This strategy is called open addressing collision resolution. 
    In particular, when the attempt is always to check the next free position in the array, it is said that
    the strategy uses linear probing.

    Implement a program that reads from the standard input operations on a HashSet 
    prints its state whenever the put and remove operations are performed.
    
    The HashSet must **store integer values** and must resolve 
    **collisions by open addressing and linear probing. 

    Your HashSet must have the following functions: 
    
            - put <value>
        - remove <value> 
        - contains <value>
        

    **To make testing easier, your HashSet will always have the following *base* hash function:

        hash(key) = key % M, where M is the size of the HashSet.

    **If the set is already completely full during an insertion, 
    simply don't add the new value. However, even if the operation is not performed,
    print the contents of the set.

     Rehashing is a topic for another issue :)

    ## Input

    Your program should read from the input the size of the table and a series of operations 
(put, remove and contains). 

        - put: adds a value to the set 
        - remove: removes the value from the set
        - contains: checks if the set contains a value passed as a parameter.

    The reading of operations must be terminated with the word `“end”`.

    ## Output

    Your program should print the contents of the HashSet whenever the put and remove operations are performed.
    When the contains operation is read, your program must print true or false.
    
    ## Restrictions

        - Your HashSet must be based on arrays. 
        - The hash function must always be the same (except for probing): key % M, 
        where M is the size of the set.
        - Create the HashSet class to organize your code. 
    
    ## Execution example
        $ javac Solution.java; java Solution
        5
        put 0
        [0, null, null, null, null]
        put 14
        [0, null, null, null, 14]
        put 20
        [0, 20, null, null, 14]
        put 0
        [0, 20, null, null, 14]
        contains 20
        true
        remove 20
        [0, null, null, null, 14]
        contains 20
        false
        end

# Adjacency matrix

    An adjacency matrix is a mathematical way of representing graphs.
    For any graph with N vertices, an NXN matrix is constructed where
    the value of M[i][j] represents the weight of the edge between the vertices represented by
    by row i and column j. For example, for an undirected graph representing
    in the figure below, we have the following
    adjacency matrix:

    ![Graph](http://www.dsc.ufcg.edu.br/~jarthur/figuras_tst_eda/grafo_nao_dirigido.png)

              a b c d e f g
            a 0 8 0 8 0 0 0
            b 8 0 5 8 0 3 0
            c 0 5 0 0 0 4 2
            d 8 8 0 0 3 3 0
            e 0 0 0 3 0 1 0
            f 0 3 4 3 1 0 5
            g 0 0 2 0 0 5 0

    As we can see, the memory usage of an adjacency matrix is not optimized.
    mainly for two reasons:

        - 1) There is repetition of information. For example, the edges between each
        pair of nodes are duplicated unnecessarily, as the graph is undirected.
        For example, the edge between `a` and `b` is represented in the matrix in the first
        row and second column and in the second row and first column.
        
        - 2) Because the matrix is square, you need to reserve space
        for all possible edges between nodes, even if they don't exist.

    Due to the nature of the hash functions we use to build Hash Tables, collisions are
    inevitable. That is, for a pair of objects with different keys, there is a possibility that their
    their hashes are the same and, consequently, these objects will be mapped to the same
    position in the table.

    One of the ways to resolve collisions is, instead of storing the <key, value> pair in a
    a position in the table, to store a queue containing all the <key, value> pairs that are
    mapped to that position.

    Implement a program that reads from the standard input operations in a 
    hash table and prints its state whenever the put and remove operations are performed.
    
    The hash table should **store integer keys and values of type String** and should resolve **collisions by chaining**.

        - put <key> <value>
        - remove <key>

        - values
        

    Important! To make testing easier, your table will always have the following hash function:

        hash(key) = key % M, where M is the size of the table

            - put: adds the key,value pair to the table

        - keys: prints the keys in the table in order. You can use Arrays.sort for this.
        - values: prints the values in the table in order. You can use Arrays.sort for this.

    Read operations must end with the word `“end”`.

    ## Output

    When the *keys* or *values* operation is read, it should print the keys or values in
    ascending order.
    
    Whenever your program reads the put and remove operations, it should
    must print the state of the table after executing these operations.

    ## Restrictions

        - Your table must be based on arrays. However, the lists within the table must be of type ArrayList.
        - The hash function must always be the same: key % M, where M is the size of the table.
        - Create the HashTable class to organize your code.

    inevitable. That is, for a pair of objects with different keys, there is a possibility that their
    their hashes are the same and, consequently, these objects will be mapped to the same
    position in the table.

    One of the ways of resolving collisions is that if the key hash is mapped to an already occupied position, the 
    position, the insertion algorithm looks for another free position to insert the <key, value> pair.
    pair <key, value>. This strategy is called open addressing collision resolution. 
    In particular, when the attempt is always to check the next position in the table, it is said that
    the strategy uses linear probing.

    **To make testing easier, your table will always have the following *base* hash function:

     Rehash is a topic for another question :)

        - keys: prints the keys in the table in order. You can use Arrays.sort for this.

question: tower_of_hanoi
statement:
# Tower of Hanoi

    Tower of Hanoi is a strategic game that has 3 vertical rods/pins (A, B and C) that work like batteries.
    
    On the first pin (A) we have disks arranged in increasing diameter (the smallest at the top).
    The aim of the game is to pass these disks to the last pin (C) with the help of the central pin (B).

    However, the game has some restrictions on movement:

        - only one disk can be moved at a time;
        - only the disk at the top of each peg can be chosen to be moved (i.e. stacked);
        - a disk with a larger diameter can never be above a disk with a smaller diameter.

    ## Input
    Your program should only read the number of discs on the first pin.

    ## Output

    Your program should display each movement of the disks, including disk origin and destination.

    ## Execution example

            $ javac Solution.java; java Solution
            2
            Moves disk 1 from stem A to stem B
            Moves disk 2 from stem A to stem C
            Moves disk 1 from stem B to stem C

question: three_n_plus_one
statement:
# 3N + 1

    Consider the following strategy for generating a sequence of 
    numbers from an integer N:

        - If N is even, divide by 2.
        - If N is odd, multiply by 3 and add 1.
        - Replace N with the generated number and repeat this process until the generated number is 1.

    For example, for N = 22, we have the following generated sequence:
        - 22 11 34 17 52 26 13 40 20 10 5 16 8 4 2 1

    Note: This is a classic programming problem. 
    It is the subject of several books on the subject. Therefore, it is not 
    authored by the teachers responsible for the tst.

    It is conjectured (there is no proof yet) that for any integer, 
    the sequence always ends in 1. However, it is known that for any integer
    between 1 and 1,000,000 this is true.

    ## Input

    Your program should read from the input two integers (one per line)
    i and j, both smaller than 1,000,000.

    ## Output

    In the output, you should print only the size of the longest sequence generated by the
    numbers between i and j (including both).


    ## Running example
    
        $ javac Solution.java; java Solution
        2
        6
        9
        $


       $ javac Solution.java; java Solution
        1
        10
        20

question: trim_linked_list

question: swap_neighbors
statement:
# Swap Neighbors

    Write a program that reads a sequence of integers and swaps the neighboring elements.
    If the length of the sequence is odd, swap the neighbors and keep the last element in
    position.


    ## Input
    
    Your program will read a sequence and store it in an array of integers.

    ## Output
    
    In the output, your program should print the array resulting from swapping the neighboring elements.

question: nearest_value_bst
statement:
# Nearest value in a binary search tree

    Write a program that reads the numbers to be added in a BST and
    a number N for which you want to find the value closest to it in the tree.

    ## Restrictions
    
        - It is not allowed to search for successors or predecessors. Even if it were, N 
        does not have to be a value present in the tree.
        - The implementation must be O(h). That is, you can't go through
        the entire tree to find the element.

    ## Input

    Your program must read two lines of input. 
    The first line will contain (in order) the elements that should be added to the tree.
    The second will contain a value N (not necessarily present in the tree). 

    Your program must find the value closest to N in the tree.

    You can assume that there will be no repeated elements in the tree.
    You can assume that no two values will be tied.

    ## Output

    Initially, your program must print out the pre-order routing of the tree read. Then, 
    print the value closest to N in the tree.
    See the execution examples below.

    ## Execution examples
    
        $ javac Solution.java; java Solution
        10 8 1 9 20 18 25
        23
        [10, 8, 1, 9, 20, 18, 25]
        25

        $ javac Solution.java; java Solution
        10 8 1 9 20 18 25
        17
        [10, 8, 1, 9, 20, 18, 25]
        18

question: circular_vector
statement:
# Circular vector

    Write a program that prints a vector in a circular fashion. 
    Your program must receive a sequence of values and an integer N and must print the N positions of the sequence read. 
    Naturally, N can be larger than the size of the sequence read. 

    In such cases, you must restart the printout again from the beginning of the vector.

    ## Input

    Your program will receive a sequence of space-separated values on the first line and, on the second line, 
    a value N that tells you how many elements should be printed.

    ## Output

    Your program should print the number sequence with N elements in a circular fashion. 
    That is, when the last element is printed, it should go back to the first and 
    continue until it reaches N printed elements.

    ## Execution examples

        javac Solucao.java; java Solucao

        6
        4 5 6 1 4 5

        javacSolucao.java; java Solucao
        3 4 2

question: word_cloud
statement:
# Word Cloud
    
    Word cloud is a graphic way of displaying the words in a given text. 
    In it, the words take on a size proportional to their frequency in the original text. So,
    a library that designs a wordcloud must use as information each word
    contained in the text under analysis and its respective frequency.


    Your goal in this question is to provide the necessary information for the word cloud builder, i.e, 
    the words and their respective frequencies. 
    To do this, implement a program that receives a String representing the text to be analyzed and returns this information.

    Important: i) consider that the string passed as a parameter is large and an O(n**2) algorithm would be impractical and 
    ii) you must choose the appropriate data structure for calculating the frequency based on what we have seen in class.

    ## Input

    Your program should read from the standard input the text to be analyzed and a sequence of word queries
    until the word `end` is read. For each query, your program should print the frequency of the term
    queried.

    You can assume that the word `end` is not part of the text to be analyzed.

    ## Output

    Your program should print its frequency for each term in the analyzed text. 
    
        ## Example of execution
        $ javac Solution.java; java Solution
        um exemplo de exemplo de texto
        um
        1
        exemplo
        2
        texto
        1
        de
        2
        end
